quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 outlook, CFO Tonya Stevens: 'we expect accelerated sequential growth, with revenue increasing 28% to $13.5 million ±$0.5 million'; at the midpoint a return to year-over-year growth, with growth driven by high-power markets and specifically AI infrastructure. Non-GAAP gross margin expected at 39.7% ±100 basis points (a 20 basis point increase at the midpoint) on a continued favorable mix shift toward high-power markets and improved scale; non-GAAP operating expenses anticipated between $15.5 million-$17.5 million. CFO: 'We continue to expect gradual improvements in gross margin throughout the year.' CEO Chris Allexandre: expanding backlogs extend beyond 2026, with record book-to-bill, supporting the expectation of continued double-digit quarterly growth through the second half and mid-single-digit revenue growth for the full year; Navitas is not guiding 2027 and gave only a directional sense of Q4.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 revenue $13.5 million ±$0.5 million (+28%); non-GAAP gross margin 39.7% ±100 basis points; non-GAAP opex $15.5 million-$17.5 million

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 detail and the opex plan, CFO Tonya Stevens: revenue was at the high end of guidance, an increase of approximately $1.9 million from $8.6 million in Q1. Operating expenses were $15.5 million (vs $15.0 million in the prior quarter and $16.1 million a year ago), at the high end of guidance as Navitas began incremental investments, particularly in new R&D programs. Loss from operations was $11.4 million (vs $11.7 million prior quarter and $10.6 million in Q2 2025); weighted average shares approximately 240.7 million; loss per share $0.04, flat to the prior quarter (vs $0.05 a year ago). Navitas is 'targeting a prudent increase of approximately $1.0 million to $1.5 million in quarterly OPEX beginning in the third quarter', roughly a 10% increase that 'remains meaningfully lower than our expected top-line growth rates' — the CFO frames it as 'in the one quarter to one-third range' of revenue growth, with a bigger step-up from Q2 to Q3 than expected afterwards; the money goes to new R&D (JFET, ultra-high-voltage SiC at 6.5 kV, 10 kV and beyond), application engineering and customer support for data-center ramps, and supply-chain readiness. CEO Chris Allexandre: the profitability goal is unchanged; with growth coming sooner than estimated, 'we decided to pull the trigger a lot faster, and that's a conscious decision.'
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 opex $15.5 million; loss from operations $11.4 million; loss per share $0.04; quarterly opex +$1.0 million to $1.5 million from Q3 (roughly 10%)

quarterly_data.signal: Revenue composition and strategy, CEO Chris Allexandre: high power now represents the majority of the revenue mix; mobile declined sequentially and year over year; both GaN and SiC contributed to sequential growth, 'with a particular acceleration in our SiC business during the quarter'; the resource reallocation and organization realignment toward high-power markets is substantially complete. Navitas made a 'deliberate strategic decision to prioritize AI infrastructure over automotive, unlike some of our competitors', and has secured initial design wins with key customers. The growth is not one large socket: 'It's tens and twenties of programs, different programs, different board, different customers' across AC/DCs, DC/DCs, BBUs, the 800 V sidecar and the compute tray — some SiC, some high-voltage or ultra-high-voltage SiC, some GaN, some both. CFO Tonya Stevens: the four high-power markets are data center and infrastructure (together AI infrastructure), performance computing and industrial electrification; Navitas does not break out revenue by them, and does not break out how much of 2027 is committed or in backlog.

800V conviction and customer engagement, CEO Chris Allexandre: 'the evolution to 800 V is inevitable, as it remains the industry's only path forward to achieve much higher power and higher density AI racks'; 'we continue to believe that the transition to 800 V architecture for next generation AI data center will happen in 2027 as various XPUs, GPUs, hyperscalers will introduce it at different times, and it will unfold in a series of steps.' Navitas is 'actively engaged with hyperscalers, merchant power customers, data centers, OEM, ODM on multiple program ramping in the second half of 2026 that will accelerate throughout 2027', with SiC and GaN being designed into DC/DC PSUs and battery backup units ahead of the 800 V transition. On native 800 V: 'We are highly confident in our position for 2027 ramp with our GaN.' On the sidecar: the mid-2027 timing 'is actually really when things accelerate'.

Product roadmap detail, CEO Chris Allexandre: GaN — the 800 V to 12 V version of the DC/DC power delivery board is in development; new programs kicked off to maximize system efficiency on the secondary side for 800 V data-center topologies; the DFN 8x8 dual-side cool package 'continues to gain broad adoption'; the 650 V 11 mΩ GaN FET 'remains the lowest RDS(on) high-voltage GaN device in the industry' (company claim), with 'a significant number of customers preparing for mass production'; medium-voltage 100 V GaN is seeing increasing adoption for the secondary side and other applications. Grid and energy: actively advancing design activity and sampling across BESS, solar farm converters, PSUs and solid-state transformers; for the recently introduced 2.3 kV and 3.3 kV GeneSiC modules 'customers have begun requesting volume samples for system-level testing in the second half of the year'; early interest in the new isolated TO-247 family for liquid cooling applications.
quarterly_data.figure: 650 V 11 mΩ GaN FET: significant number of customers preparing for mass production; 2.3 kV / 3.3 kV GeneSiC modules: volume samples requested for H2 system tests

quarterly_data.signal: Performance computing, CEO Chris Allexandre: PSU power levels in high-end computers are rising — chargers moved from 65 W and 200 W to customers now doing 200 W+ and 280 W, accelerating GaN usage; a large U.S. computing OEM's GPU-enabled notebook includes a 280 W charger 'full of GaN', at which point 'you have about $5-$6 of content of GaN'; Navitas 'just released with a customer a 1,600 W' platform powering a high-end gaming platform. This business has helped neutralize the move away from mobile ahead of the AI data center growth.
quarterly_data.figure: 280 W notebook charger: about $5-$6 of GaN content; 1,600 W gaming platform released with a customer

quarterly_data.signal: Operations and pricing: CEO Chris Allexandre — Navitas is consolidating to 'fewer, more strategic OSAT partners that are better equipped to support high power at scale' and is increasingly using AI tools across design and operations. CFO Tonya Stevens — Q2 inventory of $19.5 million compared with $14.9 million in the prior quarter; the inventory increase and wafer prepayment 'primarily reflects our measured investment to support customers' future anticipated AI data center growth'; 'channel and distributor inventory remains at healthy levels.' On pricing, the CEO: 'We've seen price increase in silicon'; he would not be specific on customer pricing — 'as tension come, you expect the pricing to go up' — but price increases in the core market have 'not been so far a focus of our side' while Navitas concentrates on customer adoption of the new architectures.

Litigation background, CEO Chris Allexandre (citing the public record): 'Wolfspeed already sued us because we stopped buying wafers from them a while back', and sued two Navitas employees who previously worked at Wolfspeed; it also tried and failed to obtain a restraining order over recruiters contacting its staff, before the GaN and SiC patent suit. The CEO said Navitas respects IP — 'We'll defend ourself' — and declined to comment on the specifics of pending litigation.

contracts.signal: CEO Chris Allexandre: 'last week, we announced a strategic partnership for Magnachip to license our GeneSiC Gen4 and Gen5 trench-assisted planar technology spanning 1.2 kV, 2.3 kV, 3.3 kV, and higher voltage'; the technology will be fully qualified and internalized in Magnachip's fab in South Korea, and Magnachip will focus on markets Navitas does not serve. The CEO said the partnership 'goes beyond the SiC'; licensing 'will, over time, play in our revenue stream' but 'this is not the prime objective' — longer term it 'facilitate establishing of another foundry source of Navitas SiC wafers'.
